props.title: Dead Air

sections.content: Dead Air belongs to the wave of post-9/11 zombie-adjacent infection films that tap into fears of bioterrorism and societal collapse. Like 28 Days Later (2002) and Right at Your Door (2006), it uses the confined space of a radio station to amplify tension as the outside world descends into chaos. The film follows radio host Logan Burnhardt (Bill Moseley) as he broadcasts during a terrorist attack that turns people into violent infected. It shares DNA with other media-focused outbreak films like Pontypool (2008), where language itself becomes the vector of infection.

sections.content: The radio station setting taps into a rich vein of broadcast-horror films like Play Misty for Me (1971) and Talk Radio (1988). These films understand the inherent drama of live broadcasting during crisis - the broadcaster becomes both narrator and participant. Dead Air particularly echoes Night of the Living Dead (1968) in its use of media reports to build dread as society crumbles. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Infection Horror

While Dead Air doesn't break new ground, it fits into the important post-millennial shift in zombie/infection narratives. Films like [REC] (2007) and Quarantine (2008) moved away from supernatural causes toward biological terrorism. This reflected real-world anxieties about anthrax attacks and dirty bombs. The confined location approach seen in Dead Air would later influence films like The Signal (2007) and Cell (2016), where modern communication technology becomes the infection vector.
